chunks: Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Ayoub, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a contracted slave who killed a man in error. He said: 'If his master, when he contracted him, had stipulated upon him that if he was unable to pay, he would return to slavery, then he is at the status of the owned slave. He is handed over to the guardians of the killed one; if they wish, they kill him, and if they wish, they sell him.'

And if his master, when he contracted him, did not stipulate upon him, and he had paid something from his contract, then Ali (peace be upon him) used to say: 'He is freed from the contract in proportion to what he has paid from his contract.'
Thus, it is upon the Imam to pay to the guardians of the killed one from the blood money in proportion to what was freed from the contract, and the blood of a Muslim man is not invalidated.

And I see that whatever remains upon the contracted slave, from what he has not paid, is slavery to the guardians of the killed one; they utilize him for his life in proportion to what remains upon him, and it is not for them to sell him.

key_terms.أَوْلِيَاءِ الْمَقْتُولِ: Guardians of the killed one (usually close male relatives)
key_terms.مُكَاتَبٍ: A slave who has entered into a contract with his master to pay a specific sum for his freedom

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a contracted slave who kills someone accidentally?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) elucidates the complex fiqh of a *mukatab* (contracted slave) who commits accidental homicide, distinguishing between cases where the master stipulated a return to slavery upon default versus those where the slave is partially freed proportionally to payments made. In the latter scenario, the Imam assumes responsibility for the blood money corresponding to the freed portion, while the remaining unpaid debt transforms the *mukatab* into a lifelong servant to the victim's heirs, who retain the right to utilize his labor but not to sell him. This ruling highlights the Shia juristic principle of preventing the nullification of a Muslim's blood (*la yabtilu damu imri'in muslimin*) through a nuanced allocation of financial and servitude liabilities. Additionally, the Imam’s reasoning reflects the broader theological emphasis on justice in *diyah* distribution, ensuring that the victim's heirs are compensated without imposing an undue burden on the state or the individual. The distinction between the master's stipulation and the Imam's adjudication underscores the dynamic role of the Imam in resolving legal ambiguities in personal status law.

en.hubeali: Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Ayoub, from Muhammad Bin Muslim who said,

‘I asked Abu Ja’far<sup>asws</sup> about a contracted slave who killed a man in error. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘If it was the case that his master had stipulated upon him when he contracted him, that if he was frustrated (from paying), so he would return it with regards to the slave, so he would be at the status of the owned slave. He would be handed over to the guardians of the killed one, so if they so desire to they can kill him, and if they so desire to they can sell him.

And if it was that his master, when he contracted him, did not stipulate upon him, and it was such that he had paid something off from his contract, so Ali<sup>asws</sup> was saying: ‘He would be free from the contract in proportionate to what he has paid off from his contract’.

Thus it would be upon the Imam<sup>asws</sup> that he<sup>asws</sup> pays the wergild to the guardians of the killed one in accordance to what he has been freed from the contract, and the blood of a Muslim person would not be invalidated.

And I<sup>asws</sup> see that whatever remains upon the contracted slave, from what he has not paid off, he would be enslave to the guardians of the killed one, to serve them for his life, in proportionate to what remains upon him, and it would not be for them that they sell him’.
